title: Trademark Law
source: Built from the Trademark Law 2311 slides (Elsa Mimoun, course coordinator), Translated Glossary and Case law list on MyCourses.

exercises.prompt: Which IP right protects an original literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, without any registration?
exercises.explain: Copyright arises without registration and lasts 70 years after the death of the author (natural person) or after divulgation by a legal person.

exercises.prompt: Match each IP right with its length of protection.
An invention can be patented if it…
choices: is new, involves an inventive step and has an industrial application
is original and fixed in a tangible form
is distinctive and capable of being represented
has an individual character and a new appearance
exercises.explain: Patent: new (not part of the prior art), inventive step (not obvious to a skilled person) and industrial application.

exercises.prompt: Copyright protection only starts once the work has been registered.
exercises.explain: Copyright is acquired without registration. Designs, patents and trademarks require registration.

exercises.prompt: "Champagne" is protected as…
exercises.explain: A PDO covers a product whose main production steps follow an established technique in one geographical area. Bayonne ham is an example of a PGI.

exercises.prompt: Since 2014 in France, "Limoges porcelain" can be protected as…
choices: a geographical indication for industrial and handcrafted products
exercises.explain: Geographical indications for industrial and hand-crafted products (GIPICP) protect non-agricultural products whose quality or reputation comes from their origin.

exercises.prompt: The infringement of an IP right is both a ___ and a ___ offense.
exercises.explain: IP infringement is both a civil and a criminal offense, and the procedure is similar for all IP rights.

exercises.prompt: What does the principle of specialty mean?
choices: A distinctive sign is only protected for the goods and services for which it is used or registered
A trademark is protected in every country
Only specialists can register a trademark
A sign is protected for all products of the company
exercises.explain: Example from the course: the sign "Sandro" is only protected for fashion items.

exercises.prompt: Match each sign with its definition.
pairs: Name under which a merchant runs his activity
Identifies the address of a website
Distinguishes the goods or services of one undertaking

exercises.prompt: A domain name is protected through a trademark infringement action (contrefaçon).
exercises.explain: Company names, commercial names and domain names have no common legislation: they are protected by an action in tort, mostly unfair competition.

exercises.prompt: A commercial name is protected against a confusing sign used for a similar activity…
choices: in the same geographical area where the merchant operates
only if it is also a registered trademark
exercises.explain: The protection of a commercial name is local: it is limited to the area where the merchant has his activity.

exercises.prompt: Which is NOT a purpose of IP rights listed in the course?
choices: Granting a permanent monopoly to the first creator
Fair competition giving consumers better services at a lower price
exercises.explain: IP rights aim at innovation, art and culture, and fair competition. Most of them are limited in time.

exercises.scenario: A competitor registers the company name "Biodermia SAS" and sells similar creams in France, creating confusion with your company "Biodermya".
exercises.prompt: Which action fits a company name?
choices: An action in tort for unfair competition
A criminal action for counterfeiting only
exercises.explain: A company name is protected in France against a confusing sign for a similar activity, through tortious liability (unfair competition).

exercises.prompt: A collective mark distinguishes…
choices: the goods and services of members of an association from those of non-members
goods certified by an independent body
one company's goods from its competitors'
products from a protected geographical area
exercises.explain: Collective marks are used by associations to identify products from several producers sharing a characteristic.

exercises.prompt: The owner of a guarantee (certification) mark may itself supply the kind of goods it certifies.
exercises.explain: Anyone can apply for a certification mark, provided they do not run a business supplying the goods or services certified.

exercises.prompt: Who can apply for an EU collective mark?
choices: Associations of manufacturers, producers, traders or service suppliers, and legal persons governed by public law
exercises.explain: Only associations and legal persons governed by public law can apply for a collective mark.

exercises.prompt: What is the application fee for an EU collective or guarantee mark?
exercises.explain: Both the EU collective mark and the EU guarantee mark cost €1,500 to apply for.

exercises.prompt: Match each mark with what it signals.
pairs: Compliance with standards set by the owner

exercises.prompt: How can a company use these marks in its CSR policy?
choices: Use a guarantee mark certifying sustainability standards it really meets
Register "eco" as an individual mark for all its products
Avoid any label to stay neutral
Use a collective mark without being a member
exercises.explain: Guarantee and collective marks signal commitment to sustainability, while trademark law prevents misleading claims.

exercises.prompt: Art. 3 TM Directive: signs capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one ___ from those of others, and of being ___ on the register.
exercises.explain: Article 3 of Directive 2015/2436 defines the trademark: any sign capable of distinguishing and of being represented on the register.

exercises.prompt: According to Hoffmann-La Roche (CJEU, 1978), the essential function of a trademark is to…
choices: guarantee the identity of origin of the product to the consumer
protect the shape of the product
exercises.explain: It lets consumers distinguish, without confusion, products of one origin from products of another origin.

exercises.prompt: Match each CJEU case with its teaching.
pairs: Use must affect the TM's functions
TM as a tool of sales promotion

exercises.prompt: Which EU text is directly applicable to the EU trademark?
exercises.explain: A regulation applies directly. Directive 2015/2436 approximates national trademark laws; Directive 2004/48 deals with enforcement.

exercises.prompt: Which international text organises the international registration of marks?
exercises.explain: The Paris Convention (1883) protects industrial property; the Madrid Protocol (1989) concerns international registration. Both are administered by WIPO.

exercises.prompt: Directive 2004/48 deals with the enforcement of intellectual property rights.
exercises.explain: It harmonises measures such as evidence seizure, right of information and remedies.

exercises.prompt: Which is NOT one of the trademark functions recognised in Bellure?
exercises.explain: Bellure: besides origin, the functions include quality, communication, investment and advertising.

exercises.prompt: The 3 conditions of the trademark definition are…
choices: any sign, capable of being represented on the register, capable of distinguishing
exercises.explain: These three conditions form the absolute grounds linked to the definition of a trademark.

exercises.scenario: Dyson applied for "a transparent bin or collection chamber forming part of the external surface of a vacuum cleaner".
exercises.prompt: What did the CJEU decide (2007)?
choices: It is not a sign: it is a mere concept
It is a valid shape mark
It is a valid colour mark
exercises.explain: Dyson (C-321/03): a concept, covering every possible shape of a transparent bin, is not a sign.

exercises.prompt: Which is NOT one of the Sieckmann criteria for the representation of a sign?
exercises.explain: Sieckmann (C-273/00): clear, precise, self-contained, easily accessible, intelligible, durable and objective.

exercises.prompt: Under Directive 2015/2436, a sign no longer has to be represented graphically.
exercises.explain: The old 2008 Directive required a graphic representation. Now the sign must be represented on the register clearly and precisely, e.g. by an audio file.

exercises.prompt: Libertel (2003): how can a colour per se be validly represented?
choices: By designating it with an internationally recognised colour code
By a paper sample of the colour only
exercises.explain: A paper sample is not durable; an internationally recognised code (e.g. Pantone) makes it clear and precise.

exercises.prompt: A mark consisting of a combination of colours without contours requires…
choices: a reproduction showing their systematic arrangement + a recognised colour code
exercises.explain: A description of the arrangement can be added but is optional.

exercises.scenario: Shield Mark tried to register the first notes of "Für Elise" and a cockcrow in several forms.
exercises.prompt: Which representation of a sound mark was accepted?
choices: A stave with clef, notes and rests
"The first nine notes of Für Elise"
The sequence of notes E, D#, E, D#, E, B, D, C, A
exercises.explain: Shield Mark (C-283/01): today a sound mark is an audio file or an accurate musical notation; onomatopoeia or bare notes are not enough.

exercises.prompt: A smell can be registered as an EU trademark if it is described by its chemical formula.
exercises.explain: Smell of ripe strawberries (T-305/04): smells cannot currently be represented with clarity and precision.

exercises.prompt: Match each type of mark with its representation.
pairs: Video file or sequential still images

exercises.prompt: A shape mark filed on paper (not electronically) may contain up to…
exercises.explain: Shape marks: graphic (incl. computer imaging) or photographic reproduction; up to six views on paper.

exercises.scenario: Linda wants to register an orange strip covering the toe area of a sock.
exercises.prompt: Which type of mark is it?
exercises.explain: A position mark shows where and in what proportion the sign is affixed, with a visual disclaimer for the rest of the product.

exercises.scenario: Georges wants to register the mooing of a cow.
exercises.prompt: Can the sign be represented?
choices: Yes, with an audio file of the sound
Only if he also files a smell
exercises.explain: An onomatopoeia is not precise enough, but an audio file is a valid representation. Distinctiveness is then a separate question.

exercises.scenario: Linda also wants to register the colour pink.
exercises.prompt: What must she file?
choices: A reproduction of the colour and a recognised colour code
A photo of a pink product
exercises.explain: A single colour requires a reproduction and a generally recognised colour code (both mandatory).

exercises.prompt: Selling bags under the sign "Bag" is…
exercises.explain: A sign is not distinctive if it is the designation of the goods (generic), describes a characteristic (descriptive) or is commonly used for them.

exercises.prompt: Place each sign on the distinctiveness scale (for bags).
A descriptive sign can still be registered if it has acquired distinctiveness through use.
exercises.explain: Acquired distinctiveness is assessed for the average consumer: surveys, market share, advertising, turnover.

exercises.prompt: Which type of sign makes the strongest trademark?
exercises.explain: The further the sign is from the goods, the more distinctive it is.

exercises.scenario: Audi applied for the slogan "Vorsprung durch Technik" (advantage through technology).
exercises.prompt: Can a slogan be a valid trademark? (CJEU, 2010)
choices: Yes, if it has some originality or resonance requiring interpretation
Only if it is in English
exercises.explain: Vorsprung durch Technik (C-398/08): a slogan is not excluded just because it conveys an objective message.

exercises.scenario: Lindt applied for the shape of its gold-wrapped chocolate bunny.
exercises.prompt: Which rule did the CJEU apply (2012)?
choices: Only a shape departing significantly from the norms of the sector is distinctive
exercises.explain: Lindt (C-98/11 P): the bunny shape did not depart enough from the customs of the sector.

exercises.scenario: Ardagh tried to register the sound of a drinks can opening.
exercises.prompt: Why was it refused (General Court, 2021)?
choices: The sound is inherent in using the goods: perceived as functional, not as an origin
It was not filed as an audio file
exercises.explain: Ardagh (T-668/19): the mark was devoid of distinctive character.

exercises.prompt: In Apple (CJEU, 2014), the layout of a retail store could be registered as a trademark.
exercises.explain: Apple (C-421/13): a store layout can be a trademark, provided it is distinctive (compare with the French Sephora case, 2000).

exercises.prompt: Which shape is NOT excluded by Art. 4(1)(e) TMD?
choices: A shape chosen for its originality, with no technical role
A shape resulting from the nature of the goods
A shape necessary to obtain a technical result
A shape giving substantial value to the goods
exercises.explain: The exclusions cover shapes resulting from the nature of goods, necessary for a technical result, or giving substantial value.

exercises.prompt: Art. 4(1)(e) prevents a ___ on technical solutions, which belong to ___ law for a limited time.
exercises.explain: Technical features belong to patents and aesthetic features to designs, both for a limited time; a trademark can last forever.

exercises.scenario: Lego registered the shape of its brick as a 3D trademark.
exercises.prompt: What did the CJEU decide (2010)?
choices: Invalid: the shape is necessary to obtain a technical result
Valid: other shapes could achieve the same result
exercises.explain: Lego Juris (C-48/09 P): the existence of alternative shapes does not save the mark; slavish copies can be fought with unfair competition.

exercises.scenario: Louboutin registered a red colour applied to the sole of a high-heeled shoe.
exercises.prompt: Was the mark valid? (CJEU, 2018)
choices: Yes: it protects a colour in a position, not exclusively a shape
No: it is a shape giving substantial value
Yes: shoes are not covered by the exclusions
exercises.explain: Louboutin (C-163/16): the main element is a colour designated by an international code, so it does not consist exclusively of a shape.

exercises.prompt: When assessing deceptive signs, the average consumer is considered particularly vulnerable to deception.
exercises.explain: The average consumer is reasonably attentive. Refusal requires actual deceit or a sufficiently serious risk of deception.

exercises.prompt: Which sign is unlawful and cannot be registered?
choices: A sign including a state flag without consent of the competent authority
exercises.explain: Unlawful signs: contrary to public policy or morality, or including flags, emblems, badges of public interest without consent.

exercises.scenario: Sarah sells cosmetics and considers the words "Beauty Cares".
exercises.prompt: What is the main risk?
choices: Refusal as descriptive / non-distinctive for cosmetics
No risk: it is the strongest option
exercises.explain: The words describe the purpose of the goods. An invented word would make a much stronger mark.

exercises.scenario: Sarah also considers "Milky care" for creams that contain no milk.
exercises.prompt: Which absolute ground could apply?
choices: Shape necessary for a technical result
exercises.explain: A sign that may mislead the public about the nature or quality of the goods is refused as deceptive.

exercises.prompt: Prior mark "Vuitton" for bags. Match each new sign with its case.
pairs: Identical sign + goods: affects a function

exercises.prompt: Which case is an exception to the principle of specialty?
choices: Similar sign creating a likelihood of confusion
exercises.explain: A reputed mark is protected even for dissimilar goods, if the use takes unfair advantage of or harms its repute or distinctiveness.

exercises.prompt: Canon (1998): likelihood of confusion is the risk that the public believes the goods…
choices: come from the same or economically linked undertakings
are sold in the same shop
exercises.explain: It includes the likelihood of association. A mere link with the prior mark is the test for reputed marks only.

exercises.prompt: Two signs are considered identical if they are the same or only show insignificant differences.
exercises.explain: Otherwise they are compared as similar signs.

exercises.prompt: Sabel (1997): signs are compared on 3 levels. Which ones?
exercises.explain: Does it look alike, sound alike, make you think of the same thing?

exercises.prompt: Which factor is NOT part of the global assessment of likelihood of confusion?
choices: The price paid for the registration
Similarity of the goods and services
exercises.explain: Factors (Sabel, Canon): similarity of signs (with dominant elements), of goods/services, distinctiveness of the earlier mark, all through the relevant public.

exercises.scenario: "Ball" is registered for copy services. Someone applies for "BALL print" for the same services.
exercises.prompt: How are the signs compared?
choices: Focus on the dominant element "BALL": the signs are similar
Only the full signs count, so no similarity
exercises.explain: More weight goes to the distinctive and dominant elements; "print" is descriptive for copy services.

exercises.prompt: To compare goods and services, which criterion is NOT taken into account?
choices: Whether they are in the same Nice class
Their end users and method of use
Whether they compete or are complementary
exercises.explain: The Nice class and the goods/services distinction are not decisive. Example: printer and printing services can be similar.

exercises.prompt: Lloyd (1999): the more distinctive the earlier mark, the higher the likelihood of confusion.
exercises.explain: Distinctiveness depends on descriptive elements, length and territory of use, promotional budget and public awareness.

exercises.prompt: The relevant public is an average consumer who is…
choices: reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, with an imperfect recollection of the mark
an expert who compares both signs side by side
exercises.explain: The level of attention varies with the goods; the consumer rarely sees both signs at once.

exercises.prompt: Where must the reputation of an earlier mark exist?
choices: In a substantial part of the country (or of the EU for an EU mark)
exercises.explain: Reputation is assessed quantitatively (knowledge by a significant part of the public) and territorially.

exercises.prompt: Which prior right is unlikely to be infringed by registering a trademark?
exercises.explain: A sign rarely conflicts with an invention. Designs, copyrights, GIs and other distinctive signs can be prior rights.

exercises.prompt: The prior TM database used in class is TM___. Relative grounds protect the rights of ___ parties.
exercises.explain: TMview lists prior trademarks. Relative grounds = infringement of third parties' prior rights.

exercises.prompt: In the EU, a trademark must be registered to give its owner an exclusive right.
exercises.explain: Art. 10 TMD: registration confers exclusive rights on the proprietor.

exercises.prompt: A well-known mark (Art. 6bis Paris Convention) is protected without registration, but its owner can only sue for…
exercises.explain: The same applies to "unregistered trademarks" (™) in common law countries.

exercises.prompt: An EU trademark registered at the EUIPO is protected in…
choices: Europe including Switzerland and the UK
exercises.explain: Principle of territoriality: national marks protect one territory; the EU mark is the exception covering the 27 states.

exercises.prompt: Online fee for a French mark in 3 classes?
exercises.explain: €190 for one class + €40 per extra class: 190 + 40 + 40 = €270.

exercises.prompt: Online fee for an EU mark in 3 classes?
exercises.explain: €850 for one class + €50 for the 2nd + €150 per additional class: 850 + 50 + 150 = €1,050.

exercises.prompt: The priority right (Art. 4 Paris Convention) gives the owner how long to file in other member countries with the same date?
exercises.explain: 179 countries are party to the Paris Convention, administered by WIPO.

exercises.prompt: Which is an advantage of the Madrid System?
choices: One form for several countries, in English, French or Spanish
exercises.explain: The applications go to each national office; the resulting marks form an "international trademark" (131 countries).

exercises.prompt: Match each procedure with what it checks.
Opposition period after publication of the application?
exercises.explain: Owners of other prior rights must wait for the registration and then ask for cancellation.

exercises.prompt: How long does a trademark registration last?
exercises.explain: There is no limit to the number of renewals.

exercises.prompt: A trademark can be revoked if it has not been genuinely used for…
exercises.explain: Revocation also applies if the mark loses its distinctiveness after registration. It can be total or partial.

exercises.prompt: The owner of a prior right who knowingly tolerated a later mark for 5 years can still ask for its cancellation.
exercises.explain: There is no general time limit for cancellation, but acquiescence for 5 successive years blocks it.

exercises.scenario: CHAMPOLLION needs TM1 in Germany, Poland, Austria, Hungary and Czech Republic.
exercises.prompt: Best route?
choices: An EU trademark at the EUIPO
exercises.explain: All five countries are EU member states, so one EU mark covers them.

exercises.scenario: CHAMPOLLION needs TM2 in France, Belgium, Switzerland and Canada.
exercises.prompt: Best route?
choices: A French (or EU) base mark extended through the Madrid System
exercises.explain: Switzerland and Canada are outside the EU: the Madrid System extends a base mark to them with one form.

exercises.prompt: For an EU trademark, who decides on cancellation or revocation at first instance?
exercises.explain: For national marks, the office or the judge can decide.

exercises.prompt: A trademark licence is a contract by which the owner…
choices: allows a third party to exploit the mark within set limits, usually for royalties
permanently transfers ownership of the mark
exercises.explain: Licensor → licensee. A permanent transfer is an assignment. Both contracts appear on the register.

exercises.prompt: Match each type of licence.
Franchising (e.g. McDonald's) is…
choices: a licence of IP rights and know-how with continuous support to replicate a business concept
exercises.explain: The franchisor provides training and support; the franchisee replicates the concept.

exercises.prompt: Which clause must an assignment agreement include, as in any sale?
choices: A warranty that the assignor is the only owner and the mark is free of burdens
exercises.explain: The price of an assignment is usually a lump sum; licences usually use royalties.

exercises.prompt: A trademark should be used as registered, both to avoid revocation and to sue for infringement.
exercises.explain: Minor changes are allowed if they do not alter distinctive character. A word mark gets wider protection (usable in figurative form).

exercises.prompt: In an international licence, how do you avoid uncertainty about the applicable law?
exercises.explain: Validity conditions vary with the applicable law, hence the governing law clause.

exercises.scenario: A garage displays "We fix BMW cars" without BMW's authorisation.
exercises.prompt: Can BMW prohibit it?
choices: No: honest use to refer to the purpose of the services
Yes: any use of a mark is infringement
Yes, if the garage is profitable
exercises.explain: Exceptions: descriptive use, use to indicate the purpose of goods/services, a person's name or address, a local prior sign.

exercises.prompt: Exhaustion of rights: the owner cannot oppose the resale of a product…
choices: put on the EEA market under the mark by him or with his consent
sold by a competitor without consent
that has been altered after sale
exercises.explain: Legitimate reasons, like altering the goods, allow the owner to oppose (guarantee of quality).

exercises.prompt: After a "saisie-contrefaçon" in France, the claimant must start the infringement lawsuit within…
exercises.explain: Art. 7 Directive 2004/48 / L. 716-4-7 IPC: measures to preserve evidence, ordered on reasonable prima facie evidence.

exercises.prompt: In France, civil trademark cases are heard by…
choices: 10 specialised tribunaux judiciaires (incl. Paris, Lille, Nanterre)
exercises.explain: Criminal cases go to the tribunal correctionnel (misdemeanour).

exercises.prompt: Maximum criminal penalty for counterfeiting in France (not in an organised group)?
exercises.explain: In an organised criminal group: up to €750,000 and 7 years.

exercises.prompt: French courts can award punitive damages in trademark cases.
exercises.explain: Damages compensate the loss (lost earnings, unfair profits, moral prejudice); there are no punitive damages in France.

exercises.prompt: To win an action in tort (passing off / unfair competition), the right holder must prove…
choices: an act, a damage and a causal link
exercises.explain: This action protects other distinctive signs and can be cumulated with infringement if a distinct prejudice is proven.

exercises.prompt: Which law applies to a trademark infringement?
choices: The law of the country where the IP right is protected
The law of the defendant's nationality
The law chosen by the claimant
exercises.explain: Courts with jurisdiction: place of the infringing act or harm, or the defendant's residence.

exercises.prompt: Match the English term with its French translation.
Match the English term with its French translation.
"Reputed trademark" in French is…
exercises.explain: Well-known trademark = marque notoire; reputed trademark = marque de renommée.

exercises.prompt: "Saisie-contrefaçon" in English is…
choices: Physical seizure of the infringing goods
exercises.explain: A judicial seizure in general is simply "seizure" (saisie judiciaire).

exercises.prompt: "Undertaking" in French means…
exercises.explain: The trademark distinguishes the goods or services of one undertaking from those of others.

exercises.prompt: Match the English term with its French translation.
Match the English term with its French translation.
"Infringement of an IP right" in French is…
exercises.explain: "Infringement of rights" in general = atteinte aux droits.

exercises.prompt: "Warranty of quiet possession clause" in French is…
choices: Clause de garantie de non éviction
exercises.explain: "Governing law clause" = clause de droit applicable.

exercises.prompt: "Misdemeanour" in French is…
exercises.explain: In France, IP infringement is a misdemeanour (délit), judged by the tribunal correctionnel.
